newsitem.title: USA: Prostate cancer more aggressive in some families.
newsitem.headline: Prostate cancer more aggressive in some families.

text.p: Prostate cancer tends to be more aggressive in men with a family history of the disease, researchers said on Monday.

In a study released at the American Urological Association annual meeting, Cleveland Clinic physicians said a nine-year study of 529 men who had undergone radical prostatectomies showed only 46 percent of those with a family history of prostate cancer remained relapse free, compared with 66 percent of those with no familial links to the disease.

"Men with a family history were significantly more likely to experience a relapse within five years after undergoing a radical prostatectomy," said Dr. Patrick Kupelian, a clinic radiation oncologist specialising in treating prostate cancer.

Kupelian told Reuters the study was the first linking poor outcome in prostate cancer patients with their family history of prostate cancer. He said he wanted to see other medical facilities complete similar studies, with more attention to family medical histories. "Once this finding is confirmed, then we can start looking at why this happens," he said.

Kupelian also said the study indicated a family history of prostate cancer may be a sign to treat a cancer more aggressively. The study did not track whether men with family histories of prostate cancer were more likely to die than others with the disease, he said.

About 350,000 new cases of prostate cancer are diagnosed each year and an estimated 42,000 men die of the disease, the clinic said. If cancer is discovered before it spreads beyond the prostate, odds of survival are significantly higher.
The American Cancer Society recommends men age 40 and older undergo annual prostate exams.
